claims.text: You can claim input tax incurred on your purchases only if all the following conditions are met:
1. You are GST-registered;
2. The goods or services are supplied to you or imported by you;
3. The goods or services are used or will be used for the purpose of your business;
4. Local purchases are supported by valid tax invoices addressed to you, or simplified tax invoices, at the time of claiming of the input tax;
5. Imports are supported by import permits that show that you are the importer of the goods and other supporting documents such as the supplier's invoices and relevant transport documents;

6. The input tax is directly attributable to taxable supplies (i.e. standard-rated supplies and zero-rated supplies), or out-of-scope supplies (e.g. third country sale of goods), that would be taxable supplies if made in Singapore;
7. The input tax claims are not disallowed under Regulations 26 and 27 of the GST (General) Regulations;

8. You have taken reasonable steps to ascertain and concluded that the goods or services were not part of a Missing Trader Fraud arrangement and the conclusion is one that a reasonable person would have made.

sources.sourceText:
You can claim input tax incurred on your purchases only if all the following conditions are met:

1. You are GST-registered;

2. The goods or services are supplied to you or imported by you;

3. The goods or services are used or will be used for the purpose of your business;

4. Local purchases are supported by valid tax invoices addressed to you, or simplified tax invoices, at the time of claiming of the input tax;

5. Imports are supported by import permits that show that you are the importer of the goods and other supporting documents such as the supplier's invoices and relevant transport documents;

6. The input tax is directly attributable to taxable supplies (i.e. standard-rated supplies and zero-rated supplies), or out-of-scope supplies (e.g. third country sale of goods), that would be taxable supplies if made in Singapore;

7. The input tax claims are not disallowed under Regulations 26 and 27 of the GST (General) Regulations;

8. You have taken reasonable steps to ascertain and concluded that the goods or services were not part of a Missing Trader Fraud arrangement and the conclusion is one that a reasonable person would have made.

When purchasing from GST-registered suppliers or importing goods into Singapore, you may have incurred GST (input tax). You can claim the input tax incurred when you satisfy all of the conditions for making such a claim. You should only claim input tax in the accounting period corresponding to the date of the invoice or import permit.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**General ECI filing deadline after financial year end** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** A company generally files ECI within three months after its financial year end unless it is specifically not required to file or qualifies for the waiver. For each Year of Assessment, the waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for the financial year and nil ECI before deducting the partial tax exemption or new start-up tax exemption. A company’s accounting profit or book loss alone does not establish nil ECI: ECI is an estimated chargeable-income amount, so the tax computation and relevant adjustments still matter. Revenue generally means income from the company’s main activity, with separate-source income excluded where it does not arise from that activity; an investment holding company’s revenue is its investment income. The company self-assesses whether it qualifies. IRAS also lists categories separately exempt from filing. To identify a particular due date, the company’s financial year end is needed; to assess a waiver, the applicable year of assessment, annual revenue and pre-exemption ECI must be known. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports General ECI filing deadline after financial year end): Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports General ECI filing deadline after financial year end): Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year;
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports General ECI filing deadline after financial year end): ECI is nil for the YA.

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports General ECI filing deadline after financial year end): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports General ECI filing deadline after financial year end): In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).

**Whether no accounting profit establishes ECI filing waiver** (party in scope: Company)

Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.

Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.

Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).

Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.

If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS

If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.

**GST zero-rating of sales to overseas customers** (party in scope: Company)

**GST distinction between exempt and zero-rated supplies** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS distinguishes zero-rated supplies, which remain taxable supplies charged at 0%, from exempt supplies, which are specifically exempted under the GST Act. outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF classification of cash allowances and official expense reimbursements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF wage treatment has two steps. First decide whether a payment is wages: CPF Board lists salary, overtime pay, bonuses, meal and transport allowances, commissions and cash incentives as examples of wages; a qualifying reimbursement for official employer expenses is excluded when it does not exceed the expense, as are specified termination benefits and non-cash benefits. Then classify wages as Ordinary Wages (OW) only when they are for employment in that month and payable by the 14th of the following month. Wages that do not meet the OW definition are Additional Wages (AW); an annual performance bonus is an example. OW and AW are both part of total wages and are subject to their applicable ceilings. Classifying a particular payment depends on what it was for, the employment month, payment timing, and, for a claimed reimbursement, the official expense and amount. A contribution calculation also requires the employee’s applicable status, age and wage facts for the relevant contribution period. [CPF | What constitutes wages for CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/what-constitutes-wages-for-cpf-contributions)

**Source:** CPF | What constitutes wages for CPF contributions (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF classification of cash allowances and official expense reimbursements): Under the CPF Act, wages are defined as remuneration in money, including any bonus that is due or granted to a person in respect of his employment.

Only payments that are considered wages should be included when declaring wage information and computing CPF contributions.

Payments to include as wages

Basic wage: Salary payable to an employee for work done.
Overtime pay: Payment to an employee for working beyond normal working hours.
Bonus: Payment such as performance bonus.
Allowance: For example, meal allowance and transport allowance.
Commission: For example, sales commission.
Cash incentive: For example, productivity incentive.

Payments not to include as wages

Termination benefit: Compensation that is not given for services or work done by the employee. For example, retrenchment benefit.
Reimbursement: Reimbursement incurred on behalf of the employer for official purposes. The reimbursement amount must not exceed the expenditure incurred. For example, purchase of office stationery.
Benefit in kind: Non-cash benefit or gift given to the employee. For example, a commemorative watch.

Classifying wages as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages

After determining that a payment is wages, classify it correctly as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages. The wage type affects how CPF contributions are computed and how the wage information should be declared.

Total Wages is the sum of Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. CPF contributions are computed on the Total Wages payable to an employee in a calendar month, subject to the applicable Ordinary and Additional Wage ceilings.

For wages to be classified as Ordinary Wages for the month, they must meet both of the following conditions:

* They are given to an employee for their employment in that month; and
* They are payable by the 14th of the following month.

For example, monthly salary.

Wages which are not classified as Ordinary Wages will be Additional Wages for the month.

For example, annual performance bonus.

The Additional Wage ceiling sets the maximum amount of AW that attracts CPF contributions in a calendar year for all employees. It is applied on a per employee, per employer, per calendar year basis.

Additional Wage ceiling calculator

Under the CPF Act, wages are defined as remuneration in money, including any bonus that is due or granted to a person in respect of his employment.

Only payments that are considered wages should be included when declaring wage information and computing CPF contributions.

Payments to include as wages

Basic wage: Salary payable to an employee for work done.
Overtime pay: Payment to an employee for working beyond normal working hours.
Bonus: Payment such as performance bonus.
Allowance: For example, meal allowance and transport allowance.
Commission: For example, sales commission.
Cash incentive: For example, productivity incentive.

Payments not to include as wages

Termination benefit: Compensation that is not given for services or work done by the employee. For example, retrenchment benefit.
Reimbursement: Reimbursement incurred on behalf of the employer for official purposes. The reimbursement amount must not exceed the expenditure incurred. For example, purchase of office stationery.
Benefit in kind: Non-cash benefit or gift given to the employee. For example, a commemorative watch.

Classifying wages as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages

After determining that a payment is wages, classify it correctly as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages. The wage type affects how CPF contributions are computed and how the wage information should be declared.

Total Wages is the sum of Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. CPF contributions are computed on the Total Wages payable to an employee in a calendar month, subject to the applicable Ordinary and Additional Wage ceilings.

For wages to be classified as Ordinary Wages for the month, they must meet both of the following conditions:

* They are given to an employee for their employment in that month; and
* They are payable by the 14th of the following month.

For example, monthly salary.

Wages which are not classified as Ordinary Wages will be Additional Wages for the month.

For example, annual performance bonus.

The Additional Wage ceiling sets the maximum amount of AW that attracts CPF contributions in a calendar year for all employees. It is applied on a per employee, per employer, per calendar year basis.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF employee coverage for part-time Singapore Citizen staff** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board generally treats a person employed in Singapore under a contract of service as an employee; full-time, part-time, temporary and contract work arrangements can qualify. Employers generally contribute for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents earning more than S$50 total wages a month. The cited guidance exempts foreigners, students who meet the stated criteria, and specified Singapore-based United Nations employees. A particular worker’s CPF coverage depends on the actual employment relationship, citizenship or PR status, monthly wages and any applicable student or organisation exemption. [CPFB | Who should receive CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/who-should-receive-cpf-contributions)

**Source:** CPFB | Who should receive CPF contributions (live external)

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF low-wage employer and employee contribution shares** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board’s computation steps use citizenship and SPR year, age group, wage band, and monthly total wages subject to the separate Ordinary and Additional Wage ceilings. For a covered employee earning wages above S$50 but not more than S$500 a month, the employee share is nil while the employer share remains due. Total contributions are rounded to the nearest dollar; cents are always dropped from the employee share. An amount cannot be established without the contribution period, current rate table, exact PR conversion and age dates, wage components, and applicable ceilings. [CPF | How much CPF contributions to pay](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay)

sources.sourceText:
Paying salary
In accordance with the Employment Act, your employer must pay your salary at least once a month and within 7 days after the end of the salary period. There are exceptions for overtime, resignation without notice and other situations.

How often salary must be paid
If you are covered by the Employment Act, your employer must pay your salary at least once a month.
They can also pay it at shorter intervals if they choose.
Salary must be paid:
Within 7 days after the end of the salary period.
For overtime work, within 14 days after the end of the salary period.

Your final salary payment could vary depending on the following situations:
In this situation | Your final salary must be paid
Employee resigns and serves the required notice period | On the last day of employment.
Employee resigns and does not serve the notice period | Within 7 days of the last day of employment.
Dismissal on grounds of misconduct | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of dismissal.
Employer terminates the contract | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of termination.

If your contract involves commission, how and when the commission is paid depends on what is in your employment contract or existing policies or practices.
If you’re a foreign employee who is leaving your employment, your employer is required to withhold all your monies due to you for tax clearance for up to 30 days upon giving notice of the cessation of your employment to the Comptroller of Income Tax. The monies include your salary, leave pay, etc.

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Part IV overtime employee coverage and minimum pay multiplier** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** MOM’s current guidance applies Part IV rules only to employees covered by Part IV; managers and executives are excluded, while contractual terms apply outside Part IV. For overtime, the stated groups are non-workmen with monthly basic pay of S$2,600 or less and workmen with monthly basic pay of S$4,500 or less; a workman generally does mainly manual labour. The non-workman overtime rate is capped at S$2,600 salary, or S$13.60 hourly. Overtime is work beyond normal hours excluding breaks and is paid at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate within 14 days after the salary period. Hourly basic pay is calculated as (12 × monthly basic pay)/(52 × 44) for monthly-rated employees, daily basic pay divided by daily working hours for daily-rated employees, and weekly basic pay divided by weekly hours for piece-rated employees. The usual cap is 72 overtime hours in a month; employers must apply for an exemption to exceed it, and MOM identifies work activities for which an exemption will not be granted. Rest-day/public-holiday work is excluded from the 72-hour count except hours beyond the usual daily hours, which count. A separate rule requires an exemption for work beyond 12 hours in a day (up to 14 hours), subject to the stated circumstances. A specific entitlement or amount depends on job duties, Part IV coverage, workman status, basic salary, normal hours, pay basis, hours worked, and applicable exemptions. The current page does not establish historical thresholds. [MOM | Hours of work, overtime and rest day](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/hours-of-work-overtime-and-rest-days)

**Source:** MOM | Hours of work, overtime and rest day (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Part IV overtime employee coverage and minimum pay multiplier): The hours of work guidelines apply only to those covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act.

Note: Part 4 of the Employment Act does not cover managers and executives.

If you are not covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act, your terms and conditions of employment will be according to your employment contract.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Part IV overtime employee coverage and minimum pay multiplier): Overtime work is all work in excess of the normal hours of work (excluding breaks).

You can claim overtime if you are:

A non-workman earning a monthly basic salary of $2,600 or less.

A workman earning a monthly basic salary of $4,500 or less.

Generally, a workman is someone whose work involves mainly manual labour. Find out if you fall under this category.

The overtime rate payable for non-workmen is capped at the salary level of $2,600, or an hourly rate of $13.60.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Part IV overtime employee coverage and minimum pay multiplier): For overtime work, your employer must pay you at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate of pay. Payment must be made within 14 days after the last day of the salary period.

A non-workman earns $2,600 a month and works 2 hours of overtime. The overtime pay is:
$13.60 × 1.5 × 2 hours = $40.80

Find out how to prevent overtime pay disputes or claims.

How overtime pay is calculated

Overtime pay is calculated as follows:

Hourly basic rate of pay × 1.5 × number of hours worked overtime

The hourly basic rate of pay is calculated as follows:

For this category of employee | Hourly basic rate of pay is

Monthly-rated employee | (12 x Monthly basic rate of pay) / (52 x 44)

Daily-rated employee | Daily pay at the basic rate / Working hours per day

Piece-rated employee | Total weekly pay at the basic rate of pay / Total number of hours worked in the week
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Part IV overtime employee coverage and minimum pay multiplier): As an employee, you are not allowed to work more than 12 hours a day.

However, your employer can ask you to work more than 12 hours a day in the following circumstances:

An accident or threat of accident.

Work that is essential to the life of the community, national defence or security.

Urgent work to be done to machinery or plant.

An interruption of work that was impossible to foresee.

Working more than 12 hours a day (overtime exemption)

If an employer requires employees to work more than 12 hours a day (up to a maximum of 14 hours), they must apply for an overtime exemption.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Part IV overtime employee coverage and minimum pay multiplier): An employee can only work up to 72 overtime hours in a month.

Employers can apply for an exemption if they require employees to work more than the 72 hours of overtime in a month.

Note: these work activities will not be granted exemption.

Note: Part 4 of the Employment Act does not cover managers and executives.

If you are not covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act, your terms and conditions of employment will be according to your employment contract.

verifiedClaims.text:
Overtime work is all work in excess of the normal hours of work (excluding breaks).

You can claim overtime if you are:

A non-workman earning a monthly basic salary of $2,600 or less.

A workman earning a monthly basic salary of $4,500 or less.

Generally, a workman is someone whose work involves mainly manual labour. Find out if you fall under this category.

The overtime rate payable for non-workmen is capped at the salary level of $2,600, or an hourly rate of $13.60.

verifiedClaims.text:
For overtime work, your employer must pay you at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate of pay. Payment must be made within 14 days after the last day of the salary period.

A non-workman earns $2,600 a month and works 2 hours of overtime. The overtime pay is:
$13.60 × 1.5 × 2 hours = $40.80

Calculate your overtime pay

Find out how to prevent overtime pay disputes or claims.

How overtime pay is calculated

Overtime pay is calculated as follows:

Hourly basic rate of pay × 1.5 × number of hours worked overtime

The hourly basic rate of pay is calculated as follows:

For this category of employee | Hourly basic rate of pay is

Monthly-rated employee | (12 x Monthly basic rate of pay) / (52 x 44)

Daily-rated employee | Daily pay at the basic rate / Working hours per day

Piece-rated employee | Total weekly pay at the basic rate of pay / Total number of hours worked in the week

- **MOM rule explanation:** MOM’s current guidance applies Part IV rules only to employees covered by Part IV; managers and executives are excluded, while contractual terms apply outside Part IV. The hours of work guidelines apply only to those covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act.

You can claim overtime if you are:

A non-workman earning a monthly basic salary of $2,600 or less.

A workman earning a monthly basic salary of $4,500 or less.

Generally, a workman is someone whose work involves mainly manual labour. Find out if you fall under this category.

The overtime rate payable for non-workmen is capped at the salary level of $2,600, or an hourly rate of $13.60.

For overtime work, your employer must pay you at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate of pay. Payment must be made within 14 days after the last day of the salary period.

A non-workman earns $2,600 a month and works 2 hours of overtime. The overtime pay is:
$13.60 × 1.5 × 2 hours = $40.80

Hourly basic rate of pay × 1.5 × number of hours worked overtime

The hourly basic rate of pay is calculated as follows:

For this category of employee | Hourly basic rate of pay is

Monthly-rated employee | (12 x Monthly basic rate of pay) / (52 x 44)

Daily-rated employee | Daily pay at the basic rate / Working hours per day

Piece-rated employee | Total weekly pay at the basic rate of pay / Total number of hours worked in the week

As an employee, you are not allowed to work more than 12 hours a day.

However, your employer can ask you to work more than 12 hours a day in the following circumstances:

An accident or threat of accident.

Work that is essential to the life of the community, national defence or security.

Urgent work to be done to machinery or plant.

An interruption of work that was impossible to foresee.

Working more than 12 hours a day (overtime exemption)

Note: these work activities will not be granted exemption.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Managers and executives excluded from Part IV overtime coverage** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** MOM’s current guidance applies Part IV rules only to employees covered by Part IV; managers and executives are excluded, while contractual terms apply outside Part IV. For overtime, the stated groups are non-workmen with monthly basic pay of S$2,600 or less and workmen with monthly basic pay of S$4,500 or less; a workman generally does mainly manual labour. The non-workman overtime rate is capped at S$2,600 salary, or S$13.60 hourly. Overtime is work beyond normal hours excluding breaks and is paid at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate within 14 days after the salary period. Hourly basic pay is calculated as (12 × monthly basic pay)/(52 × 44) for monthly-rated employees, daily basic pay divided by daily working hours for daily-rated employees, and weekly basic pay divided by weekly hours for piece-rated employees. The usual cap is 72 overtime hours in a month; employers must apply for an exemption to exceed it, and MOM identifies work activities for which an exemption will not be granted. Rest-day/public-holiday work is excluded from the 72-hour count except hours beyond the usual daily hours, which count. A separate rule requires an exemption for work beyond 12 hours in a day (up to 14 hours), subject to the stated circumstances. The hours of work guidelines apply only to those covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act.

Note: Part 4 of the Employment Act does not cover managers and executives.

If you are not covered under Part 4 of the Employment Act, your terms and conditions of employment will be according to your employment contract.

Overtime work is all work in excess of the normal hours of work (excluding breaks).

You can claim overtime if you are:

A non-workman earning a monthly basic salary of $2,600 or less.

A workman earning a monthly basic salary of $4,500 or less.

Generally, a workman is someone whose work involves mainly manual labour. Find out if you fall under this category.

The overtime rate payable for non-workmen is capped at the salary level of $2,600, or an hourly rate of $13.60.

For overtime work, your employer must pay you at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate of pay. Payment must be made within 14 days after the last day of the salary period.

A non-workman earns $2,600 a month and works 2 hours of overtime. The overtime pay is:
$13.60 × 1.5 × 2 hours = $40.80

Calculate your overtime pay

Calculate your overtime pay

Find out how to prevent overtime pay disputes or claims.

How overtime pay is calculated

Overtime pay is calculated as follows:

Hourly basic rate of pay × 1.5 × number of hours worked overtime

The hourly basic rate of pay is calculated as follows:

For this category of employee | Hourly basic rate of pay is

Monthly-rated employee | (12 x Monthly basic rate of pay) / (52 x 44)

Daily-rated employee | Daily pay at the basic rate / Working hours per day

Piece-rated employee | Total weekly pay at the basic rate of pay / Total number of hours worked in the week

As an employee, you are not allowed to work more than 12 hours a day.

However, your employer can ask you to work more than 12 hours a day in the following circumstances:

An accident or threat of accident.

Work that is essential to the life of the community, national defence or security.

Urgent work to be done to machinery or plant.

An interruption of work that was impossible to foresee.

Working more than 12 hours a day (overtime exemption)

If an employer requires employees to work more than 12 hours a day (up to a maximum of 14 hours), they must apply for an overtime exemption.

An employee can only work up to 72 overtime hours in a month.

Employers can apply for an exemption if they require employees to work more than the 72 hours of overtime in a month.

Note: these work activities will not be granted exemption.

Work on rest day or public holidays is not counted in the 72-hour overtime limit, except for work done beyond the usual daily working hours on those days. Such extra hours are included in the 72-hour limit.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Part IV monthly overtime-hours limit and exemptions** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** MOM’s current guidance applies Part IV rules only to employees covered by Part IV; managers and executives are excluded, while contractual terms apply outside Part IV. For overtime, the stated groups are non-workmen with monthly basic pay of S$2,600 or less and workmen with monthly basic pay of S$4,500 or less; a workman generally does mainly manual labour. The non-workman overtime rate is capped at S$2,600 salary, or S$13.60 hourly. Overtime is work beyond normal hours excluding breaks and is paid at least 1.5 times the hourly basic rate within 14 days after the salary period. Hourly basic pay is calculated as (12 × monthly basic pay)/(52 × 44) for monthly-rated employees, daily basic pay divided by daily working hours for daily-rated employees, and weekly basic pay divided by weekly hours for piece-rated employees. The usual cap is 72 overtime hours in a month; employers must apply for an exemption to exceed it, and MOM identifies work activities for which an exemption will not be granted. Rest-day/public-holiday work is excluded from the 72-hour count except hours beyond the usual daily hours, which count. A separate rule requires an exemption for work beyond 12 hours in a day (up to 14 hours), subject to the stated circumstances. A specific entitlement or amount depends on job duties, Part IV coverage, workman status, basic salary, normal hours, pay basis, hours worked, and applicable exemptions. The current page does not establish historical thresholds. [MOM | Hours of work, overtime and rest day](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/hours-of-work-overtime-and-rest-days)

outcomes.question: How many months after closing the accounts does a listed company get for its AGM compared with a non-listed company?

issues.subject: AGM deadlines after financial year end by listed status

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**AGM deadlines after financial year end by listed status** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s current guidance states that, for financial years ending on or after 31 August 2018, listed companies generally hold an AGM within four months after FYE and non-listed companies within six months. A private company may be exempt if it sends its financial statements to all members within five months after FYE, or if it is dormant, not listed (and not a subsidiary of a listed company), and has assets of S$500,000 or less (consolidated for an ultimate parent). It may also dispense with an AGM by a resolution passed by all members. Even then, a member can request an AGM up to 14 days before the six-month deadline; the company must hold it within six months after FYE. A member or auditor may request a general meeting within 14 days of receiving the financial statements, and the company must hold that meeting within 14 days of the request. The page says an extension application must be made before the due date but does not state its duration or all conditions. AGM details must be declared in the annual return even if no AGM was held. A specific conclusion depends on FYE, listing/private status, dormancy, group status, assets, delivery of statements, resolutions, requests and any extension application. [ACRA | Due dates & requirements for annual general meetings (AGMs)](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/holding-annual-general-meetings/due-dates-requirements/)

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** Additional case facts or checks are required; see the issue-level limitations.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Private-company AGM exemption and member meeting-request safeguards** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s current guidance states that, for financial years ending on or after 31 August 2018, listed companies generally hold an AGM within four months after FYE and non-listed companies within six months. A private company may be exempt if it sends its financial statements to all members within five months after FYE, or if it is dormant, not listed (and not a subsidiary of a listed company), and has assets of S$500,000 or less (consolidated for an ultimate parent). It may also dispense with an AGM by a resolution passed by all members. Even then, a member can request an AGM up to 14 days before the six-month deadline; the company must hold it within six months after FYE. A member or auditor may request a general meeting within 14 days of receiving the financial statements, and the company must hold that meeting within 14 days of the request. The page says an extension application must be made before the due date but does not state its duration or all conditions. AGM details must be declared in the annual return even if no AGM was held. A specific conclusion depends on FYE, listing/private status, dormancy, group status, assets, delivery of statements, resolutions, requests and any extension application. [ACRA | Due dates & requirements for annual general meetings (AGMs)](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/holding-annual-general-meetings/due-dates-requirements/)

**ACRA annual-return duty of dormant companies despite IRAS tax waiver** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s current guidance requires each company that remains live with ACRA to file an annual return each year, including an inactive or dormant company and a company granted an IRAS tax-filing waiver. The current deadline is five months after FYE for a listed company or seven months for a non-listed company; the corresponding period is six or eight months if the company has share capital and an overseas branch register. Company name and registration number

Details of directors, the company secretary, and members

**Annual-return overseas branch-register exception by listed status** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s current guidance requires each company that remains live with ACRA to file an annual return each year, including an inactive or dormant company and a company granted an IRAS tax-filing waiver. **Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Company facts needed to determine next AGM deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s current guidance states that, for financial years ending on or after 31 August 2018, listed companies generally hold an AGM within four months after FYE and non-listed companies within six months. A private company may be exempt if it sends its financial statements to all members within five months after FYE, or if it is dormant, not listed (and not a subsidiary of a listed company), and has assets of S$500,000 or less (consolidated for an ultimate parent). It may also dispense with an AGM by a resolution passed by all members. Even then, a member can request an AGM up to 14 days before the six-month deadline; the company must hold it within six months after FYE. A member or auditor may request a general meeting within 14 days of receiving the financial statements, and the company must hold that meeting within 14 days of the request. The page says an extension application must be made before the due date but does not state its duration or all conditions. AGM details must be declared in the annual return even if no AGM was held. A specific conclusion depends on FYE, listing/private status, dormancy, group status, assets, delivery of statements, resolutions, requests and any extension application. [ACRA | Due dates & requirements for annual general meetings (AGMs)](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/holding-annual-general-meetings/due-dates-requirements/)

**Source:** ACRA | Due dates & requirements for annual general meetings (AGMs) (live external)

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**LFMC quarterly financial return forms and deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS’s 29 May 2026 SFA compliance toolkit states that an LFMC files quarterly Forms 1 and 2 within 14 days after each quarter end under Regulation 27 of the FMR. It also lists annual audited Forms 1 to 6 and the audited Profit and Loss Account, Balance Sheet and auditor’s report (including a management letter, if any) within five months after financial year end under section 107 of the SFA and Regulation 27 of the FMR. The toolkit says it is non-exhaustive and excludes obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. Confirm the entity’s LFMC scope, reporting period, and current MAS-Tx instructions before applying these deadlines. A complete reporting calendar also needs the licence and manager regime, regulated activities, fund types and reporting periods, plus checks for event-triggered notifications and duties outside this toolkit. One quarterly financial return does not establish that all MAS duties are discharged. [LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit-lfmcs29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

**Source:** LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports LFMC quarterly financial return forms and deadline): This compliance toolkit aims to provide LFMCs with a simple reference on the common applications, forms and submissions pursuant to the SFA that are applicable to LFMCs. However, it is not exhaustive, and LFMCs are expected to be familiar with all legislations and requirements that are applicable to them. For the avoidance of doubt, this toolkit excludes reporting obligations that fall outside the SFA; as well as fund-level requirements (e.g. Code of Collective Investment Scheme). Where an LFMC intends to apply for or holds a CMS licence to carry on business in other SFA regulated activities such as dealing in Capital Markets Products, it should also refer to the compliance toolkit that is relevant to these other types of regulated activities. LF MCs are welcomed to provide suggestions on this toolkit using the Guided Form at Contact Us. Relevant to: | LFMCs

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** Additional case facts or checks are required; see the issue-level limitations.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**LFMC audited annual financial return documents and deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS’s 29 May 2026 SFA compliance toolkit states that an LFMC files quarterly Forms 1 and 2 within 14 days after each quarter end under Regulation 27 of the FMR. It also lists annual audited Forms 1 to 6 and the audited Profit and Loss Account, Balance Sheet and auditor’s report (including a management letter, if any) within five months after financial year end under section 107 of the SFA and Regulation 27 of the FMR. The toolkit says it is non-exhaustive and excludes obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. Confirm the entity’s LFMC scope, reporting period, and current MAS-Tx instructions before applying these deadlines. A complete reporting calendar also needs the licence and manager regime, regulated activities, fund types and reporting periods, plus checks for event-triggered notifications and duties outside this toolkit. One quarterly financial return does not establish that all MAS duties are discharged. outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**LFMC name or principal-business-place change notification** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS’s 29 May 2026 SFA toolkit says an LFMC must notify MAS within 14 days after a change of name or principal place of business, using a Notice for Change in Particulars under section 93 of the SFA. This rule is for the LFMC entity changes shown in the toolkit; confirm LFMC status, the change date, and current submission instructions. The toolkit is non-exhaustive and excludes fund-level and non-SFA reporting. outcomes.question: Can a venture capital fund manager simply use the normal LFMC financial-return checklist without checking its own regime?
outcomes.subject: VCFM versus ordinary LFMC reporting applicability

issues.subject: VCFM versus ordinary LFMC reporting applicability

outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**VCFM versus ordinary LFMC reporting applicability** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** The cited toolkit addresses ordinary LFMC reporting. A VCFM must check its own applicable framework; the ordinary LFMC financial-return checklist cannot be transplanted automatically. MAS’s 29 May 2026 SFA compliance toolkit states that an LFMC files quarterly Forms 1 and 2 within 14 days after each quarter end under Regulation 27 of the FMR. It also lists annual audited Forms 1 to 6 and the audited Profit and Loss Account, Balance Sheet and auditor’s report (including a management letter, if any) within five months after financial year end under section 107 of the SFA and Regulation 27 of the FMR. The toolkit says it is non-exhaustive and excludes obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. Confirm the entity’s LFMC scope, reporting period, and current MAS-Tx instructions before applying these deadlines. A complete reporting calendar also needs the licence and manager regime, regulated activities, fund types and reporting periods, plus checks for event-triggered notifications and duties outside this toolkit. One quarterly financial return does not establish that all MAS duties are discharged. outcomes.answer:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence is incomplete for one or more material issues.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** Additional case facts or checks are required; see the issue-level limitations.
**Material evidence gaps:** See the evidence gaps and coverage limitations below.

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Verified evidence; case application unresolved

**Facts needed for MAS regulatory reporting calendar and completeness** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS’s 29 May 2026 SFA compliance toolkit states that an LFMC files quarterly Forms 1 and 2 within 14 days after each quarter end under Regulation 27 of the FMR. It also lists annual audited Forms 1 to 6 and the audited Profit and Loss Account, Balance Sheet and auditor’s report (including a management letter, if any) within five months after financial year end under section 107 of the SFA and Regulation 27 of the FMR. The toolkit says it is non-exhaustive and excludes obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. Confirm the entity’s LFMC scope, reporting period, and current MAS-Tx instructions before applying these deadlines. A complete reporting calendar also needs the licence and manager regime, regulated activities, fund types and reporting periods, plus checks for event-triggered notifications and duties outside this toolkit. One quarterly financial return does not establish that all MAS duties are discharged. [LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit-lfmcs29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

claims.text: This compliance toolkit aims to provide LFMCs with a simple reference on the common applications, forms and submissions pursuant to the SFA that are applicable to LFMCs. However, it is not exhaustive, and LFMCs are expected to be familiar with all legislations and requirements that are applicable to them. For the avoidance of doubt, this toolkit excludes reporting obligations that fall outside the SFA; as well as fund-level requirements (e.g. Code of Collective Investment Scheme). Where an LFMC intends to apply for or holds a CMS licence to carry on business in other SFA regulated activities such as dealing in Capital Markets Products, it should also refer to the compliance toolkit that is relevant to these other types of regulated activities. LF MCs are welcomed to provide suggestions on this toolkit using the Guided Form at Contact Us. Relevant to: | LFMCs
